questions: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?

lines.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
lines.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.

has_statements: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences.

quick_question.q: How did a study link ketamine trips to near-death experiences?
options: By comparing words in written reports
By scanning people's brains on ketamine
quick_question.why: A computer compared words in about 15,000 online drug reports and 625 near-death accounts. Nobody was given ketamine.

questions: What side effects does MDMA cause in therapy trials?

lines.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
lines.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.

quick_question.q: Of the minor problems listed in MDMA trial records, how many made it into the published papers?
quick_question.why: More than half of the minor problems, and 4 serious ones, never made it into the published papers.

questions: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?

lines.short: Tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, two reviews say. So the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.
lines.but: The reviews give no numbers. Not how long a break must be, or how much the risk of a fatal overdose rises.
how: The older review offers this as a possible explanation. It says tolerance may fade quickly, and not at the same pace for every effect. But there's little data on how fast.
The idea rests on one hair study. People who died of heroin overdose had less morphine in their hair than people still using. The review reads that as less use before death.
The newer review gives prison and detox as examples of a break; the older one, which it cites, doesn't.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

questions: Does music change how a ketamine treatment session goes?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
lines.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.

questions: How common are bad trips, and can problems last?

lines.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
lines.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 said they'd thought of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.

57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But people who hadn't used them weren't asked, so it's unknown how many would have had these anyway.

quick_question.q: In a US survey, how many in 100 people who used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip?
quick_question.why: 41 in 100 recalled one, looking back over their whole life in an online survey. Most were still glad they had used psychedelics.

questions: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

has_statements: After Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use as a crime in 2001, drug use fell.

quick_question.q: Portugal's crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year. Mainly why?
options: Possession stopped counting as a crime
quick_question.why: Possession for your own use stopped counting as a crime in 2001, so those cases left the arrest count.

questions: Do take-home fentanyl strips match what trained staff find?

lines.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
lines.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In British Columbia in 2019, people took strips from ten harm-reduction sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 on site; cocaine, 17 against 1. The authors think most extra positives were false, but didn't test it.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.

quick_question.q: When people tested opioids with take-home fentanyl strips, how many in 100 results showed fentanyl?
quick_question.why: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 tested by staff. People reported results, often from memory.

questions: Does MDMA-assisted therapy help PTSD more than therapy with a dummy pill?

lines.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused talking therapy.

quick_question.q: In MDMA trials, how many in 10 finishing on a dummy pill plus therapy no longer had PTSD?
quick_question.why: 3 to 5 in 10 on a dummy pill with the same therapy no longer had PTSD, against about 7 in 10 on MDMA.

questions: Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?

lines.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.

quick_question.q: In a psilocybin quit-smoking study, most weren't smoking 6 months later. How many took part?
quick_question.why: Just 15 people, and 12 weren't smoking. All got psilocybin plus lots of counselling, with no comparison group.

questions: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?

lines.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
lines.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published 1991 to 2002, of 11,505 students in grades 5 to 12, comparing those who had DARE with those who didn't.
Students who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as others. The studies checked from right after the classes to 10 years later.
In 8 of the 11 studies, the result couldn't be told apart from no difference. Two small ones found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more.
Four results, including the only 10-year one, weren't worked out but filled in as zero.

has_statements: Kids who had the original DARE classes went on to use less alcohol, tobacco and drugs than other kids.

quick_question.q: A 2004 review found DARE had no clear effect on alcohol, tobacco or drug use. Which version?
quick_question.why: All 11 studies tested the original classes. DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.

questions: How fast can you get hooked on cocaine?

lines.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
lines.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence. So did about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.

quick_question.q: Within a year of starting, how many people who used only powder cocaine met the criteria for dependence?
quick_question.why: For people who went on to crack it was about 22 in 100; the survey cannot show that crack made the difference.

questions: How many people who use stimulants like meth get hooked?

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

quick_question.q: In an old US survey, which drug had the most people ever dependent per 100 who used it?
quick_question.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, alcohol 15, stimulants like meth about 11; there is no figure for meth alone.

questions: Is low blood salt after MDMA more common in women?

lines.short: Yes, among people who got ill: 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men, in one poison-centre study.
lines.but: It counts only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Only 188 of 545 people in California poison-centre records had a blood salt test. Of 105 women tested, 55 had a low level; of 83 men, 18 did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.
A review describes 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount: a marker of a water-holding hormone rose only in women, with no clear difference reported in the hormone or blood salt.

quick_question.q: Among people ill after taking MDMA who had a blood test, who more often had low blood salt?
quick_question.why: 52 in 100 women against 22 in 100 men. These were people who became ill, not everyone who takes MDMA.

questions: Do cannabis medicines help long-lasting pain?

lines.short: Slightly: about half a point less pain out of 10 than with a dummy medicine.
lines.but: The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with long-lasting pain got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
Pain scores were about half a point lower out of 10 with the medicine.
37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%; this difference may be due to chance.
Most of the combined trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, and none lasted more than 15 weeks.

quick_question.q: In trials, how much did cannabis medicines lower long-lasting pain on a 0-to-10 scale, versus a dummy?
quick_question.why: About half a point lower than with a dummy. The trials were short and mostly tested one mouth spray.

questions: Is teenage cannabis use linked to depression or anxiety later?

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most were a bit more often depressed later than teens who didn't.
lines.but: These studies can't show that cannabis caused it; other differences between the teens may explain it.
how: Seven long-term studies followed teens who did and did not use cannabis until they were young adults.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. The studies did not say how many in 100 became depressed.
The studies took into account how depressed or anxious the teens were at the start, but not always tobacco or other drugs.
Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only three studies measured it.

questions: Is strong cannabis more closely linked to psychosis than weaker cannabis?

lines.short: Daily use of strong types had the strongest link with psychosis, but the gap from weaker types could be chance.
lines.but: Strength was guessed from the type people named, and both studies come from one team.
how: Two studies by one team, one in south London and one in 11 places in Europe and Brazil, compared people who had a first psychosis with people from the same areas who had not.

In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong types (10% THC or more on average) went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis, compared with never using. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times; the gap between the two could be chance.

In the 11 places, using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis. In London, using strong types less than once a week went with nearly 2 times the odds, but some numbers in that study do not add up. In both studies, weaker types were not linked once all patterns of use were counted together.
Nobody tested the cannabis: people named the type they had used after they became ill, and its strength was taken from police, European and national figures.

has_statements: In two studies linking strong cannabis to psychosis, researchers tested the cannabis people had used.

quick_question.q: In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong cannabis went with what odds of psychosis?
options: About the same as those who never used
About 50 times those who never used
About 5 times those who never used
quick_question.why: About 5 times; daily use of weaker types, about 2 times. The gap between strong and weaker types could be chance.

questions: Is teenage cannabis use linked to suicidal thoughts or attempts?

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.
lines.but: Only three studies each, mostly measured in the teen years; they cannot show cause.
how: A review combined three long-term studies on suicidal thoughts and three on suicide attempts.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and about 3.5 times the odds of attempts, compared with teens who did not use cannabis.
In two of the three studies for each, this was measured while the young people were still teenagers.
In other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were taken into account.

questions: Will I sleep badly when I stop cannabis?

lines.short: Studies in one review found that many people who used cannabis regularly sleep badly after stopping, often with strange dreams.
lines.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Studies asked people how they slept after stopping regular cannabis, and some recorded their sleep in a lab.
Between about a third and three quarters of those with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks.
In the lab they took longer to fall asleep and woke up more than before they stopped.
Poor sleep was linked with going back to cannabis.

questions: Does memory recover after people stop using ecstasy?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether scores recover after people stop using ecstasy.
lines.but: The studies compared different people, not the same people over time.
how: A review pooled a few small studies of people who had stopped for at least 6 months.
They scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used.
Breaks longer than 6 months were not tested, although the review's summary says otherwise.
Most of the studies were rated poor quality.

questions: Do brain scans show serotonin changes in people who use ecstasy?

lines.short: Scans show less of a serotonin marker in people who use ecstasy.
lines.but: Nobody in these studies was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.
how: The marker sits on the endings of serotonin nerve cells in the brain.
Four teams used the same scan and all found less of it in the outer brain.
Deeper parts of the brain mostly looked the same as in other people.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.

questions: What is serotonin syndrome, and how do doctors spot it?

lines.short: Doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking, sweating and restlessness when serotonin may be too high.
lines.but: The checklist was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses, against that unit's own diagnosis.
how: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) is too much serotonin activity, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. It ranges from mild to severe.
Doctors examine the person for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.
In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs matched the unit's diagnosis in about 84 of 100 people diagnosed. An older checklist matched about 75 of 100.
Everyone had taken an overdose, and mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects. No independent test of the checklist was found.

has_statements: Mild signs of serotonin syndrome (too much serotonin activity) can look like ordinary drug effects.

quick_question.q: Which signs do doctors look for to spot serotonin syndrome, caused by drugs that raise serotonin?
quick_question.why: Muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness; when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.

questions: Can a benzodiazepine sleeping pill affect my driving the next day?

lines.short: Some benzodiazepine sleeping pills made people drive worse the next day than after dummy pills.
lines.but: Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.
how: Volunteers drove a real car or a driving machine the day after a pill or a dummy pill.
Researchers measured how much the car weaved inside its lane.
With some pills the weaving was worse than with alcohol at the driving limit used in several countries.
With other pills or lower doses, weaving was not clearly different from dummy pills, but each result came from one small study.

has_statements: A benzodiazepine sleeping pill at bedtime can't affect your driving the next day.

quick_question.q: The day after some benzodiazepine sleeping pills, how did lane weaving compare with alcohol at a driving limit?
options: About half as bad as the alcohol
quick_question.why: With some pills, weaving was worse than with alcohol at a limit several countries use. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers.

questions: Is using LSD, mushrooms or mescaline linked to mental health problems?

lines.short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.
lines.but: People were asked once, so the survey can't show whether LSD, mushrooms or mescaline cause or prevent problems.
how: 130,152 US adults answered private computer questions at home in 2001 to 2004; 21,967 had ever used LSD, mushrooms, mescaline or peyote.
At first glance, all 20 mental health measures were 2 to 3 times as common in people who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline.
Those who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline used far more other drugs: 98 in 100 had used cannabis, against 33 in 100 of others.
Once that, risk-taking, stressful events and background were counted, no measure was higher for LSD, mushrooms or mescaline. A few were lower, maybe by chance.

has_statements: In a US survey, people who used LSD or mushrooms still had more mental health problems once other differences were counted.

quick_question.q: In a US survey, what erased the mental health gap for people who'd used LSD or mescaline?
options: Counting their other drug use and life stress
Leaving out people who used only once
quick_question.why: Once other drug use, risk-taking and stressful events were counted, none of 20 measures was higher. Asked once, the survey can't show cause.

questions: Does a second dose work like the first?

lines.short: A second dose raises the drug in your blood, but not the strongest feeling.
lines.but: Three small laboratory studies, 9 to 23 people, and none gave more than two doses.
how: Blood levels rose more than the extra dose alone explains: MDMA slows its own breakdown.
The strongest feeling was no stronger after the second dose, but it lasted about an hour longer.
Heart rate hardly rose further, while blood pressure and body temperature did.
No study worked out how much effect a given blood level should give.

questions: Does caffeine make you sharper, or just undo withdrawal?

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

has_statements: In a lab study, caffeine made people who have it often more alert than people who rarely have it.
In one study, caffeine made people who often have it more alert than people who rarely do.

quick_question.q: In people who rarely have caffeine, what did caffeine change in a lab study?
quick_question.why: They got faster and more jittery, not more alert. One study.

questions: Why do some people on methadone feel withdrawal before their next dose?

lines.short: In one small study, their methadone level tended to drop faster after its daily high point.
lines.but: Only 18 people were tested for one day, and by our check the difference fell just short of statistical significance, even after the authors left two people out.
how: Nine people who felt withdrawal before their next dose were compared with nine who did not.
Just before the dose, both groups had about the same level of methadone in their blood.
On average, in both groups, withdrawal was lowest in the hours after the dose and grew as the level fell.
The study did not test any change to treatment.

quick_question.q: Just before the next dose, how did methadone blood levels compare in people with and without withdrawal?
options: Much lower in those with withdrawal
Much higher in those with withdrawal
quick_question.why: About the same. In those with withdrawal, the level tended to drop faster after its daily high; only 18 people were tested.

questions: Can I get flashbacks after LSD or psilocybin?

lines.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
lines.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.

has_statements: In lab studies, about 1 in 11 volunteers reported a short flashback after LSD or psilocybin.

quick_question.q: In lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, what was a flashback usually like?
options: A few seconds of changed seeing
Hours of living through the whole trip again
A vision problem that never went away
quick_question.why: Most came in the days after, usually lasting seconds, and nobody was found with a lasting vision problem.

questions: Why do some bodies, or some medicines, make MDMA stronger?

lines.short: MDMA seems to switch off the enzyme that clears it, so body differences matter less.
lines.but: Only 7 people had no working enzyme, and no study gave a second dose of MDMA.
how: Among 139 volunteers in eight lab studies, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 had a peak MDMA level about 15 percent higher, in the first 3 hours only.
In 15 men, tests after one MDMA dose looked like those of people with no working enzyme in 10 of them. The enzyme had not fully recovered after 10 days.
Medicines that block the enzyme raised the MDMA peak by about 15 to 20 percent. Paroxetine raised it by 16 percent in 12 men.
Bodies that differ are one reason a person can feel little from an amount and take more. None of these studies gave a second dose, so what happens then is not known.

questions: What about other psychiatric medicines?

lines.short: Few other psychiatric medicines were tested with MDMA, and the results differ by medicine.
lines.but: Each was tested once in 14 to 16 healthy people, and the results come second-hand from a 2022 review.
how: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, did not change heart rate or blood pressure. It lowered well-being by about 31 percent and raised anxiety by about 47 percent.
Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rise in heart rate by about 79 percent.
The review found no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA.
A slow start, as with methylphenidate, can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. No trial tested what happens then.

questions: What did the 'Rat Park' studies show about environment and drugs?

lines.short: Less than is often said. Rats living together drank less morphine water, but only in some tests.
lines.but: All of this was in rats, so it says nothing direct about people.
how: In 1979, by the last test, rats kept alone drank 5 to over 16 times as much sweet morphine water as rats living together.
In 1978, when morphine water was almost all they had to drink, the rats living together drank more of it.
In all three studies, the two groups drank morphine water from different machines, measured differently. That could explain part of the gap.
Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result.

has_statements: In the 1978 Rat Park study, rats living together refused morphine water.

quick_question.q: Two later experiments tried to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study. What happened?
options: They found the same big difference
They did not find the same result
They found an even bigger difference
quick_question.why: The result was not repeated. In the original studies the two groups were also measured differently, and all were rats.

questions: How many opioid deaths also involve alcohol?

lines.short: Alcohol was listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
lines.but: Alcohol is often left off death records, and these counts do not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008.
Alcohol was listed more often in men's deaths (17 in 100) than in women's (about 10 in 100).
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged alcohol involved in about 12 in 100 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Without knowing how many people drink with opioids, these counts cannot say how much alcohol adds to risk. Two reviews describe no study in people that measured it.

quick_question.q: US death records listed alcohol in about how many in 100 opioid overdose deaths?
quick_question.why: Death certificates listed alcohol in about 15 of 100, but alcohol is often left off death records.

questions: Does LSD damage your chromosomes?

lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
lines.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.

has_statements: Studies of people given pure LSD found clearly more broken chromosomes.
The early studies that linked LSD to broken chromosomes ruled out other drugs.

quick_question.q: Where did the 1967 LSD chromosome scare come from?
options: Cells from two people in a dish
Tests on thousands of people who used LSD
Babies born to mothers who took LSD
quick_question.why: Cells from two people in a dish: LSD was added to their blood cells in a lab. Cells in a dish aren't people.

questions: Do people throw drugs away when a test shows something unexpected?

lines.short: Sometimes. At one festival, 67 in 100 people handed over drugs that were not as sold.
lines.but: That was one festival, where chemists tested the drugs. After a strip showed fentanyl, few did.
how: At an English festival in 2016, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not as sold handed drugs over to be destroyed.
When the drug matched, 15 of 164 did. Staff saw these handovers, but people may have kept other drugs.
At a supervised injection site, people said they would throw the drug away after 11 in 100 checks that showed fentanyl, and after 7 in 100 that did not.
A review of drug checking services printed rates of 0 to 10 in 100 from four studies.

has_statements: Most people throw their drugs away when a fentanyl test strip shows fentanyl.

quick_question.q: At one festival, when tests showed drugs were not as sold, how many in 100 handed them over?
quick_question.why: 30 of 45 people handed drugs over to be destroyed, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched. One festival, with chemists testing.

questions: Do 'smart drugs' like Adderall make healthy people smarter?

lines.short: Barely. A single pill of Adderall (amphetamine) or methylphenidate gave healthy adults at most a small lift on some lab tests. In one trial, people felt helped; scores didn't rise.
lines.but: These studies tested a single pill in a lab, in healthy volunteers. Daily use, studying and exams were not tested.
how: In a US trial, 46 healthy young adults took Adderall or a dummy pill on different test days. None of 13 tests improved.
They still rated the Adderall pill as more helpful than the dummy pill, but feeling helped was not clearly linked to scoring better.
Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response.
A bigger boost to memory tested hours or days later came mostly from one lab's studies of men. Adjusted for missing studies, it nearly halved.

has_statements: In one trial, healthy adults' test scores rose after taking Adderall.

quick_question.q: In studies of healthy adults, what did a single pill of methylphenidate or amphetamine do to thinking?
options: Gave a small lift on some tests
Gave a big lift on most tests
Made scores worse on most tests
quick_question.why: A small average lift, clearest for holding back an automatic response; memory gains shrank after allowing for unpublished studies.

questions: Do most US dollar bills carry traces of cocaine?

lines.short: In one US study, about 9 in 10 one-dollar bills had traces of cocaine. The typical bill held a little over a millionth of a gram.
lines.but: One small study of 50 US one-dollar bills collected by 2000. Cocaine on money today, or elsewhere, may differ.
how: The bills came from everyday purchases, 10 each in Baltimore, Chicago, Denver, Honolulu and San Juan. Only 4, all from Chicago, had no cocaine.
One bill from Honolulu held about 7 in 10 of all the cocaine found. So the average was far above what most bills held.
A few bills also carried heroin (7 of 50), methamphetamine (3) or PCP (2).
No people were tested here. The author doubts handling these bills could make you fail a urine test, citing one person in an older study.

has_statements: In one US study, most one-dollar bills had traces of cocaine.

quick_question.q: Of all the cocaine on 50 US dollar bills, how much was on the bill with the most?
quick_question.why: About 7 in 10 sat on one Honolulu bill, so the average was far above what most bills held.

questions: How often is chest pain after cocaine a heart attack?

lines.short: US studies looked at people in hospital with chest pain after cocaine. About 1 to 6 in 100 were having a heart attack.
lines.but: These were 1990s studies, and their blood tests could miss small heart attacks.
how: One US hospital kept everyone with chest pain after cocaine in for a day of blood tests. 6 in 100 were having a heart attack.
In 136 heart attacks after cocaine, no one died in hospital. About half the problems, like an uneven heartbeat, were there on arrival.
A year after a hospital visit, 3 in 100 had died, none of a heart attack; 1 in 100 had a heart attack and lived.
The few later heart attacks were all in people who said they still used cocaine: 2 in one study, 4 in another.

has_statements: In US hospitals, most people with chest pain after cocaine were having a heart attack.

quick_question.q: Of people tracked a year after cocaine-linked chest pain, 3 in 100 died. How many from heart attacks?
quick_question.why: None of the deaths were from a heart attack; 1 in 100 had a heart attack and lived.

questions: How many opioid deaths also involve benzodiazepines?

lines.short: About 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017 also involved benzos.
lines.but: Death records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths does not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed benzos in 21 of 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 9 in 1999.
Benzos were listed more often with prescription opioids or methadone (about 1 in 3) than with heroin or fentanyl.
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged benzos involved in about 6 in 10 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Of people on prescribed opioids who died of overdose, half (US veterans) to three in four (Ontario) had benzo prescriptions.

has_statements: Among people on prescribed opioids who died of overdose, half to three in four also had benzo prescriptions.

quick_question.q: In 2017 US death records, about how many in 100 opioid overdose deaths also involved benzos (calming medicines)?
quick_question.why: Death certificates listed benzos in 21 of 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 9 in 1999.

questions: Is using ketamine linked to bladder problems?

lines.short: Ketamine is linked to bladder problems seen in over 4,000 patients. In one survey, about 1 in 4 people who used it blamed it for urine problems.
lines.but: No study compared how often people who use ketamine and people who don't get these problems. So none can show ketamine caused them.
how: In over 4,000 patients seen by doctors, mostly in Asia, about 77 in 100 needed to pee often and 60 in 100 had bladder pain.
In about 3 in 10 of these patients, urine had backed up and swollen a kidney. About 8 in 100 had weaker kidney function.
The survey was online, mostly in the UK: 1,285 people who had used ketamine in the past year. Those who used more reported more symptoms.
Of 251 people who described how symptoms changed, 128 said they eased after stopping. No study compared people who stopped with those who kept using.

has_statements: In one survey of people who used ketamine, about 1 in 4 blamed it for urine problems.

quick_question.q: In one survey, what did people say happened to bladder symptoms after they stopped ketamine?
options: Many got better, but not all
quick_question.why: 128 of 251 survey respondents said they got better after stopping. No study compared them with people who kept using.

questions: How many cancers are caused by alcohol?

lines.short: A model estimated that drinking caused about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
lines.but: It is a computer estimate, not a count. It applies risks from studies of groups of people to every country.
how: Researchers combined how much people drink in each country with cancer risks from earlier studies. They compared this with a world where no one had ever drunk.
They estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer made up the most.
Most were linked to more than 20 g of alcohol a day, about two drinks. About 103,000 were linked to less than that.
The model counted only harms, for the cancers an international agency lists. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths from alcohol in 2004.

quick_question.q: How many in 100 new cancers worldwide did a model estimate were caused by drinking?
quick_question.why: The model estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women.

questions: Is moderate drinking linked to changes in the brain?

lines.short: In one UK study, people who drank more alcohol more often had a memory area rated 'shrunken' on a scan. So did 35 in 100 who barely drank.
lines.but: Each brain was scanned once, so the study shows a link, not shrinking, and not that alcohol caused it.
how: 527 UK government workers, mostly men, reported how much alcohol they drank over 30 years, then had one brain scan around age 70.
'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. Even 35 in 100 people who barely drank alcohol got that rating.
The paper's 'three times the odds' came from the top of its 'moderate' range for men; lower down, the study was too small to tell.
Only one of three thinking tests (naming words that start with a letter) fell slightly faster with more drinking. No test at the scan differed.

has_statements: A UK study scanned people's brains over 30 years and saw them shrink as people drank more alcohol.

quick_question.q: How many people who barely drank alcohol had a 'shrunken' memory area in a UK scan study?
quick_question.why: About 35 in 100 did. People who drank more got the rating more often, but one scan can't show alcohol caused it.

questions: What are the DTs (delirium tremens), and how often do they happen?

lines.short: Sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal; a few in 100 people in hospital get it.
lines.but: Most figures are passed on by one review or come from old trials, mostly one from 1969.
how: The DTs are confusion that comes on fast and comes and goes, together with signs of withdrawal such as shaking or a fast pulse.
A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after withdrawal begins and last 2 or 3 days. It says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them.
In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who got dummy pills developed delirium. Most of these people were in one trial from 1969.
The review says about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. It names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs they are more likely.

has_statements: A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after alcohol withdrawal begins.

quick_question.q: In hospital for alcohol withdrawal, how many in 100 people get the DTs, a sudden confusion?
quick_question.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them. Most figures come from that review or old trials.

questions: Is drinking coffee linked to better or worse health?

lines.short: Mostly better: in studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often. In pregnancy, and for women's bones, the links went the other way.
lines.but: These studies only watched people, and gene studies found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.
how: A big review gathered the research on coffee and health. Most of it came from studies that followed people for years.
People who drank coffee had lower rates of death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and, most of all, liver disease.
In pregnancy, more coffee was linked to low birth weight and losing the pregnancy. Women who drank more had more fractures; men had fewer.
A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked; people who smoke tend to drink more coffee.

has_statements: In studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often.

quick_question.q: In people who had never smoked, how was coffee linked to lung cancer?
quick_question.why: No clear link: it disappeared in people who never smoked. People who smoke tend to drink more coffee.

questions: If I suddenly go without my usual caffeine, will I get a headache?

lines.short: Without their usual caffeine, half got a headache by evening; people given caffeine pills did not.
lines.but: Only 40 hospital patients took part, and surgery itself can also cause headaches.
how: 40 people who drank lots of caffeine had to stop it before a small operation.
Half got caffeine pills and half got identical dummy pills, and neither the patients nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which.
By evening, 10 of the 20 with dummy pills had a headache, and none with caffeine.

quick_question.q: Before surgery, people who drank lots of caffeine got dummy pills instead. How many had headaches by evening?
quick_question.why: 10 of the 20 on dummy pills had a headache by evening; none given caffeine pills did. Only 40 hospital patients took part.

questions: Is cannabis in pregnancy linked to smaller babies or intensive care?

lines.short: Babies were a bit lighter, and more of them went to intensive care after birth.
lines.but: Many mothers also smoked or drank. Most studies could not tell this apart from cannabis.
how: Researchers combined 19 studies, mostly from before 2000. They compared babies of mothers who did and did not use cannabis while pregnant.
Babies of mothers who used cannabis weighed about 109 grams less. More of them went to newborn intensive care.
It is not clear whether they were born early more often. Birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common.
Most studies did not keep tobacco and alcohol apart from cannabis. So they cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.

quick_question.q: Babies of mothers who used cannabis while pregnant: how did they compare with other babies?
options: No difference in weight or care
A bit lighter; more went to intensive care
Heavier; fewer went to intensive care
quick_question.why: About 109 grams lighter, and more went to newborn intensive care. But many mothers also used tobacco or alcohol.

questions: Does cocaine narrow heart arteries, and do beta-blockers make it worse?

lines.short: Yes, in a lab cocaine narrowed heart arteries a little. After a beta-blocker, blood flow fell further in all 10 patients, but its effect on heart attacks is unknown.
lines.but: No trial has ever tested beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine.
how: That lab test used 10 heart patients who had never used cocaine. The beta-blocker, propranolol, went straight into a heart artery.
In 2008, US heart doctors advised against beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine. That rests mainly on small lab tests, animal tests and expert opinion.
In hospital records of about 2,000 people, heart attacks and deaths were not clearly different with beta-blockers. But doctors chose who got them.
Two reviews counted one cocaine study's blood tests as heart attacks or damage. That study of 58 people reported no heart complications or deaths.

has_statements: The warning against beta-blockers after cocaine is based on big trials.

quick_question.q: In a lab, what happened to heart blood flow when 10 people got the beta-blocker propranolol after cocaine?
quick_question.why: It fell in all 10 heart patients. None had used cocaine before.

questions: How common is cocaine psychosis among people treated for cocaine use?

lines.short: 68 in 100 people treated for cocaine reported psychotic symptoms; 16 in 100 had a diagnosed disorder.
lines.but: These were people in treatment, and many also used alcohol or other drugs.
how: One review pooled 17 studies of 5,286 people, mostly in treatment for cocaine in the US and Spain.
Asked about symptoms such as paranoia, 68 in 100 said they had had them with cocaine. Strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100.
The review could not separate cocaine from the alcohol and other drugs people used, so it cannot show cocaine alone caused it.
Other studies the review cites say the symptoms usually pass after stopping, but can get worse with more use and last for weeks.

has_statements: Studies cited in a review say symptoms such as paranoia with cocaine usually pass after stopping.

quick_question.q: Among people treated for cocaine use, how many said they had had symptoms such as paranoia with cocaine?
quick_question.why: A review of 17 studies; strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100.

questions: Do people who use test strips have fewer overdoses?

lines.short: No one knows yet. One study found no clear difference over four weeks.
lines.but: The result was too uncertain to rule out fewer or more overdoses.
how: One US study followed 732 people at harm-reduction sites for four weeks in 2023. Once other differences were allowed for, overdoses that people survived were about as common in people who used strips as in those who did not.
That comparison also allowed for safety steps people took during the study, which could hide a difference. Before anything was allowed for, overdoses looked twice as common in people who used strips.

In Baltimore, 103 women were given strips, and 68 were asked again about 8 weeks later. 6 said they had an overdose in the month before the start, and 1 in the month before the last visit. There was no comparison group, and women who used no strips also reported fewer.
A review of 91 research papers found only two that looked at overdoses, and neither compared people who tested with people who did not.

has_statements: People who use fentanyl test strips have been shown to have fewer overdoses.

quick_question.q: In Baltimore, women given fentanyl test strips reported fewer overdoses later. What about those who used none?
quick_question.why: They also reported fewer. Overall, 6 said they had an overdose in the month before the start, 1 before the last visit; no comparison group.

questions: Do official counts miss drug deaths?

lines.short: Some deaths are missing; others are counted without showing which drug was involved.
lines.but: The gaps differ by place and rules. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.
how: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 out of 100 overdoses had only an unspecified-drug code.
Models guessed which drugs those counted deaths involved. They did not find deaths missing from the total.
In Stockholm, lists with similar totals disagreed about which people to include. They used different rules.
An England and Wales estimate suggests counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It did not match each death across lists.

quick_question.q: In US death records from 1999 to 2015, how many overdoses had no specific drug named?
quick_question.why: About 23 out of 100 had only an 'unspecified drug' code. The gaps differ by place and rules.

questions: Does memory improve when people cut down or stop frequent ketamine use?

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. People who had stopped did as well as people who don't use it.
lines.but: The people who had stopped had mostly used less, and nobody was tested before starting.
how: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well on memory tests as people who don't use ketamine. They still did a year later.
But most of them had used less than the people who used most days, so this does not show that stopping fixed anything.
In 18 people who had cut down, one word test caught up after 3 to 4 years. Story memory and speed stayed lower, as at their first test.
People who were still using also scored better on average a year later, perhaps partly from practice.

quick_question.q: In one study, people had quit ketamine for at least a month. How did their memory scores compare?
options: Far below people who don't use it
As good as people who don't use it
A bit below people who don't use it
quick_question.why: As good, still a year later. But most had used less to begin with, so stopping may not be why.

questions: Does ketamine affect memory and thinking that night, and 3 days later?

lines.short: That night, memory scores were far below other partygoers'. Three days later the gap was mostly gone.
lines.but: Two small studies by one team, and nobody tested what people had taken.
how: People were tested within half an hour of taking ketamine. They remembered less than half as much of a short story as people at the party who had not taken it.
They felt strongly cut off from their body and surroundings, numb, and as if time had changed.
Three days later, at home, their attention scores matched the other group's, and most of these feelings had gone. In one of the two studies, feeling detached was still higher.
Some memory scores were still lower. People may have remembered little of the first test, so had less practice. Or the groups were different to begin with.

quick_question.q: Tested soon after taking ketamine at a party, how much of a short story did people remember?
options: Less than half as much as others
quick_question.why: Less than half as much as partygoers who had not taken it. Nobody tested what people had taken.

questions: How often is kratom found in overdose deaths?

lines.short: Kratom turned up in about 6 of every 1,000 overdose deaths in 27 US states in 2016–17. It was almost always found with other drugs.
lines.but: Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some deaths with kratom were probably missed.
how: A CDC system gathered 27,338 overdose deaths from 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017. Kratom was found in 152.
Kratom was named as a cause in 91 deaths. Other drugs turned up in 84 of them; fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.
Only 7 deaths had kratom as the only drug found. Even then, the report says other drugs cannot be ruled out.
The system counts mostly deaths where opioids played a part. With no count of people who use kratom, there is no death rate.

has_statements: In death records from 27 US states, most deaths where kratom was named as a cause had no other drug found.

quick_question.q: In 27 US states in 2016–17, how many overdose deaths had kratom found in them?
quick_question.why: 152 of 27,338 deaths. Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some were probably missed.

questions: Is using ecstasy in pregnancy linked to birth defects?

lines.short: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy in pregnancy, but it cannot show cause.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, and almost half of the enquiries were lost to follow-up.
how: A UK information service followed 136 pregnancies in which ecstasy was used, nearly all in the first 3 months. 62 of them also involved other drugs.
Of 78 babies born alive, 12 (about 15 in 100) had a birth defect, a mix of minor and major ones. The authors expected 2 to 3 in 100.
Two babies had heart defects and three had a twisted foot. The authors say the study is too small to confirm a link with any one defect.

A later study followed babies of 28 women who used ecstasy but did not report a count of birth defects. One baby had a rare genetic condition, which the authors say cannot be tied to the mother's drug use.

quick_question.q: In one UK study, how many in 100 babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had a birth defect?
quick_question.why: About 15 in 100, against 2 to 3 expected. But there was no comparison group, and almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up.

questions: Is meth use linked to crime?

lines.short: People dependent on meth reported more crime in months when they used it.
lines.but: One study, and it could not show which came first.
how: In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth were followed for up to three years. Each person's months with meth were compared with their own months without.
Some crime was reported in 56 of 100 months with meth use and about 18 of 100 without.
The link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime. It stayed after other drug use and money and housing problems were counted.
People reported use and crime for the same months, and treatment or time in prison was not counted.

quick_question.q: In one study of people dependent on meth, which crimes were most linked to months of use?
quick_question.why: Selling drugs and property crime, even after money and housing problems were counted; the study can't show which came first.

questions: Does the antidepressant mirtazapine help people use less meth?

lines.short: In three trials, people on a depression medicine, mirtazapine, used somewhat less meth than on a dummy pill.
lines.but: Most people kept using, and in the largest trial drug tests showed no difference.
how: Two small San Francisco trials, in men who have sex with men who also had counselling, found fewer meth-positive urine tests on mirtazapine.
A larger Australian trial: people said they cut down by about 2 more days in 4 weeks.
Its saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most people kept using.
Drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine.

quick_question.q: In the largest trial of mirtazapine for meth, people said they used less. What did saliva tests show?
options: No difference from a dummy pill
Much less use than on a dummy pill
More use than on a dummy pill
quick_question.why: No difference, though people said they cut down by about 2 more days in 4 weeks; most kept using.

questions: Is meth linked to psychosis?

lines.short: Psychotic symptoms are more common in people who use meth, most of all in those who use it often.
lines.but: No study has settled which comes first.
how: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about 2.5 times the odds of psychosis.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth: use went with slightly more psychotic experiences.
In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years. Among people with no drug record, it was under 1 in 100.
None of these studies shows which came first.

quick_question.q: In Taiwan, how many adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs like meth got psychosis diagnoses within 10 years?
quick_question.why: An estimated 4 in 100 in Taiwan, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record; this can't show which came first.

questions: Have meth use and meth deaths risen in the US?

lines.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
lines.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.

quick_question.q: In the US, deaths involving meth were about 550 in 1999. About how many were there in 2023?
quick_question.why: About 35,000, though many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids.

questions: Does melatonin help children on ADHD medicine fall asleep?

lines.short: Children on ADHD medicine fell asleep about 16 minutes sooner with melatonin than with a dummy pill.
lines.but: This was one small study of 19 children, paid for by the company that made the melatonin.
how: Each child took melatonin on some nights and a dummy pill on others, without knowing which.
Doctors did not see a bigger overall improvement with melatonin than with the dummy pill.
Reported health problems were mild or moderate, apart from one severe migraine, and about as common with the dummy pill.
All the children had first tried a bedtime routine that had not fixed their sleep.

quick_question.q: How much sooner did children on ADHD medicine fall asleep with melatonin than with a dummy pill?
quick_question.why: About 16 minutes, in one small study of 19 children paid for by the company that made the melatonin.

questions: What does stopping smoking feel like, and for how long?

lines.short: After stopping smoking, people can feel grumpy, anxious and restless, and wake more at night, for weeks.
lines.but: This comes from one expert's summary of older studies; it does not say how many people get each feeling.
how: The studies asked the same people how they felt before and after they stopped smoking.
Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks.
Feeling tired, headaches and sweating did not go up after stopping.
For some people the feelings lasted longer or came back after about three weeks.

has_statements: In older studies, headaches and sweating went up after people stopped smoking.

quick_question.q: After stopping smoking, when were most feelings like grumpiness and restlessness strongest, in older studies?
quick_question.why: Most were gone within 2 to 4 weeks, but for some people they lasted longer or came back.

questions: Can a bad reaction to PCP last for weeks?

lines.short: In three reported cases, a severe breakdown lasted two to four weeks, then passed.
lines.but: Only three cases from 1975, and nobody tested the drugs they had taken.
how: Three young men were treated in one hospital after street drugs thought to contain PCP.
They were confused, angry and unsteady, two heard voices, and one jumped from a high window.
All three got better, and afterwards remembered little of their illness.
Earlier studies the doctors cited said the mind effects of PCP usually last about a day.

quick_question.q: In three reported cases after drugs thought to contain PCP, how long did a severe breakdown last?
options: Two to four weeks, then it passed
For the rest of their lives
quick_question.why: Two to four weeks, then it passed in all three. Only three cases from 1975, and nobody tested the drugs.
